pinboard.title: How Complex Systems Fail
pinboard.description:
How Complex Systems Fail
(Being a Short Treatise on the Nature of Failure; How Failure is Evaluated; How Failure is Attributed to Proximate Cause; and the Resulting New Understanding of Patient Safety)
Richard I. Cook, MD
Cognitive Technologies Labratory
University of Chicago
Complex systems are intrinsically hazardous systems.
All of the interesting systems (e.g. transportation, healthcare, power generation) are inherently and unavoidably hazardous by the own nature. The frequency of hazard exposure can sometimes be changed but the processes involved in the system are themselves intrinsically and irreducibly hazardous. It is the presence of these hazards that drives the creation of defenses against hazard that characterize these systems.
...
Views of ‘cause’ limit the effectiveness of defenses against future events.
Post-accident remedies for “human error” are usually predicated on obstructing activities that can “cause” accidents. These end-of-the-chain measures do little to reduce the likelihood of further accidents. In fact that likelihood of an identical accident is already extraordinarily low because the pattern of latent failures changes constantly. Instead of increasing safety, post-accident remedies usually increase the coupling and complexity of the system. This increases the potential number of latent failures and also makes the detection and blocking of accident trajectories more difficult.

pinboard.title: Behind Jensen Huang’s spy scandal, a shadow war for Trump’s ear on China Rubio’s intervention helped topple one of Washington’s most influential corporate voices on China, giving momentum to officials pushing for tougher restrictions.
pinboard.description:
As Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang gained extraordinary access to President Donald Trump and secured his blessing to sell artificial intelligence chips to China, he fueled a backlash among Washington officials and national security hawks who wanted to keep the powerful technology out of Beijing’s hands.

Some national security officials within the Trump administration chafed at Huang’s influence over the president, according to two former officials.

Huang’s downfall, which has the potential to mark a dramatic shift in power, was ultimately set in motion by one of the capital’s most influential China hard-liners, national security adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Rubio issued a memo warning Trump about the relationship between Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, based on a report generated by the CIA, according to a person familiar with the matter. Rubio used the CIA report to write his own, recasting the agency’s reporting in his own more assertive terms, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe confidential intelligence.

When the findings of Rubio’s memo — swiping at one of Trump’s closest allies — leaked in news reports, they set off a chain of events that culminated in Huang’s resignation Thursday.

Huang admitted to and apologized for having an affair with an executive at an Nvidia customer, who American spies suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board launched an investigation, but Huang ultimately resigned following reports of another affair with a subordinate.

After Huang’s resignation, Trump referred to him as a “legend” who had “done a fantastic job.”

At a Group of Seven summit in Paris this week, Rubio declined several times to answer reporters’ questions on his role in alerting the White House to Huang’s affair.

When asked if the allegations of Chinese spying changed his views on negotiating with Beijing over the future of AI, Rubio said, “The Chinese system is always going to act in the best interest of the Chinese system, and the United States will always act in the best interest of the United States. I work for the American people.”

The ouster marks a huge victory for those who had long sought to curb Huang’s influence over Trump’s policy toward Beijing, and a stunning turn in a shadow battle that has raged for years between Nvidia and those in Washington who see China as a military and technology threat.

Huang’s “China hawk” opponents — a bipartisan group of government officials, lawmakers and think tank analysts — view Nvidia’s chips as a vital asset in the rivalry between the two nations and one that the U.S. should strictly control.

Until recently, Huang’s close relationship with Trump appeared to give him the upper hand. But with the downfall of the leather-jacket sporting CEO, the hawks are ready to seize on the moment to redirect the national agenda toward tougher policies on China.

In Congress, China hard-liners are working to insert new restrictions on China’s access to chip into a major defense bill they hope to pass by the end of the year.

Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Michigan), the chairman of the House Select Committee on China and a figure who has long tangled with the chipmaker, said Congress should advance legislation to further restrict the traffic in chips and called on Nvidia’s new leaders to prioritize national security.

“Jensen Huang’s firing from the company he founded is an unfortunate end that could have been avoided,” Moolenaar said in a statement. “It is in our national interest for NVIDIA and our other AI champions to succeed, but American companies should never jeopardize our nation’s security by giving Chinese companies access to their most advanced chips.”

Many of Trump’s national security team had not shared the president’s view on exports of chips, according to a former official who worked on chips policy and is still connected to the industry, who likened Huang’s relationship to handing officials a “nuclear bomb.”

“They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president,” said the former official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal dynamics.
